title: Interval List Intersections
statement:
You get two lists of closed intervals, `firstList` and `secondList`. An interval `[start, end]` covers every real number `x` with `start <= x <= end`. Within each list the intervals are sorted by `start` and none of them overlap or touch.

Return the intersection of the two lists: the numbers covered by both lists, written as disjoint closed intervals `[start, end]` sorted by `start`. Each piece is where one interval of `firstList` overlaps one interval of `secondList`, and a piece may be a single point `[p, p]`. If the lists share no number, return an empty list.
constraints: Within each list, every interval ends strictly before the next one starts
notes:
## Intuition

You could compare every interval of one list with every interval of the other, but that is O(n·m). Both lists are sorted, so the overlaps appear in order, like merging two sorted arrays. Look at the current interval of each list. Whichever one ends first cannot overlap anything later in the other list, because those later intervals start after the current one ends. So it is safe to drop it and move on.

## Approach

1. Start pointers `i` and `j` at the first interval of each list, with an empty `result`.
2. While both pointers are in range, the overlap of the two current intervals runs from `start`, the larger of the two starts, to `end`, the smaller of the two ends.
3. If `start <= end`, the overlap is non-empty (possibly a single point), so append `[start, end]`.
4. Advance the pointer whose interval ends first. On a tie, advancing either one is fine.
5. When either list runs out, no more overlaps are possible; return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

- `[0,2]` and `[1,5]` give `[1,2]`; `2 < 5`, so `i` moves.
- `[5,10]` and `[1,5]` give `[5,5]`; `j` moves.
- `[5,10]` and `[8,12]` give `[8,10]`; `i` moves.
- `[13,23]` and `[8,12]`: `start = 13 > end = 12`, no overlap; `j` moves.
- `[13,23]` and `[15,24]` give `[15,23]`; `i` moves.
- `[24,25]` and `[15,24]` give `[24,24]`; `j` moves.
- `[24,25]` and `[25,26]` give `[25,25]`; `i` moves past the end.

The result is `[[1,2],[5,5],[8,10],[15,23],[24,24],[25,25]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m): every step advances one pointer.
- Space: O(1) besides the output, which holds at most `n + m` intervals.

## Pitfalls

- The intervals are closed, so `start === end` is a real overlap; use `<=`, not `<`.
- Move the pointer by comparing **ends**, not starts. The interval that ends later may still overlap the next interval of the other list.
- One list may be empty; the loop condition already returns `[]` in that case.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `result` | the overlaps found so far, in order |
| `i`, `j` | current interval in `firstList` and `secondList` |
| `start` | the later of the two current starts |
| `end` | the earlier of the two current ends |

narration.3: i points at the current interval of firstList...
narration.4: ...and j at the current interval of secondList.
narration.5: Overlaps are only possible while both lists still have intervals.
narration.6: An overlap cannot begin before the later of the two starts.
narration.7: It must stop at the earlier of the two ends.
narration.8: A non-empty overlap (even a single point) needs start <= end.
narration.9: Record it; overlaps come out sorted because both lists are.
narration.11: Does the first list's interval end first?
narration.12: Then it cannot meet any later interval of the second list, so drop it.
narration.14: Otherwise drop the second list's interval, which ends no later.
narration.17: One list is used up, so every overlap has been found.
